=== Project 58777.pdf ===
Project No. 58777

Submitted by: Thomas L. Darte

Date: February 3, 2026

Introduction

This filing provides additional explanation and context for my prior submission
(https://interchange.puc.texas.gov/Documents/58198_12_1513572.PDF) introducing a
Texas‑style market design intended to support the construction of dispatchable
generation. As noted in my testimony before the Senate Business and Commerce
Committee on March 4, 2025, during consideration of SB 388, Texas urgently needs a
market structure capable of attracting sustained investment in new generation consistent
with the ERCOT Reliability Standard.

My interest in grid reliability extends back to my service as chairman of an ERCOT Board
subcommittee that developed reliability recommendations in 1999–2000, and more
recently through multiple filings following the 2021 winter storm. The LSERO with Bilateral
Contracting builds on those decades of experience and offers a practical, competitive, and
Texas‑appropriate solution.

LSERO With Bilateral Contracting

“LSERO with Bilateral Contracting creates a uniquely competitive structure in which
wholesale competition directly “feeds” into retail competition. Unlike centralized capacity
markets that produce a single clearing price, LSERO with Bilateral Contracting allows each
LSE to procure its own reliability obligation from any qualified supplier. Because every LSE
has a different load shape, a different mix of renewables, storage, and demand‑side
resources, and a different risk profile, each bilateral contract will reflect unique
competitive conditions. GENCOs must compete for each LSE’s business, and LSEs are
free to buy from multiple suppliers or individual units. These decentralized, competitive
transactions ensure that no single capacity price can emerge and that competitive forces
at both wholesale and retail levels will drive delivered electricity toward cost‑of‑service
outcomes.”

“While no market can ever be entirely free of market‑power influences, the LSERO with
Bilateral Contracting is designed to be highly resistant to them. Because each LSE has a
unique reliability obligation and is free to procure from any qualified supplier, wholesale
competition directly feeds into retail competition. GENCOs must compete for each LSE’s
business, and any seller that attempts to overprice will simply lose contracts to rivals or
new entrants. Combined with oversight from the IMM, ERCOT, and federal antitrust
 authorities, this decentralized structure minimizes the potential for market‑power abuse
far more effectively than centralized capacity markets that rely on a single clearing price.”



Executive Summary

LSERO with Bilateral Contracting offers several advantages that make it well suited to
Texas:

•     Simple and practical. The structure is easy to understand and straightforward to
implement.

•      Eliminates reliance on scarcity pricing. There is no need to “chase scarcity price
spikes” to support investment.

•      Avoids PCM complexities. Bilateral contracts are well‑established financial
instruments that provide predictable revenue streams for generation developers.

•     Enhances competition rather than regulation. GENCOs compete to supply the next
increment of dispatchable capacity needed to meet the ERCOT Reliability Standard.

•     Clear and fair allocation. Each LSE receives a defined reliability obligation—
metered sales being one possible basis—and can meet that obligation through any
combination of resources, including renewables, storage, and demand‑side options.

•       Wholesale competition feeds retail competition. The decentralized nature of
bilateral procurement ensures that competitive pressures at wholesale flow directly into
retail pricing.

•     Supports cost‑of‑service outcomes. Complete freedom to contract allows
competitive forces to drive delivered electricity toward cost‑of‑service levels, benefiting all
Texans.

The LSERO with Bilateral Contracting provides a market‑based, Texas‑appropriate
mechanism to support the construction of new dispatchable generation while preserving
retail choice and minimizing market‑power risks.



Respectfully submitted,

Thomas L. Darte

February 3, 2026
 

=== PUC letter 2-3-26.pdf ===
Chairman Thomas J. Gleeson and Commissioners                                    2/3/26

Public Utility Commission of Texas

1701 N. Congress Avenue

Austin, Texas 78701

Chairman Thomas J. Gleeson and Commissioners,

My name is Thomas L. Darte, and I am writing to respectfully request that the Commission
place on a future Open Meeting agenda my proposed market design using a LSERO with
Bilateral Contracting framework to be sent to ERCOT for formal evaluation. I submit this
request in my personal capacity, informed in part by my prior service as a member of the
ERCOT Board. My interest in Texas grid reliability spans several decades, including earlier
work on ERCOT reliability issues and more recent engagement following the 2021 winter
storm. I have also submitted a filing in Project No. 58777 providing additional explanation
of the LSERO with Bilateral Contracting and its application to the ERCOT Reliability
Standard. This proposed solution “differs completely and uniquely” from the LSERO
proposed in the Nov 2022 study by E3 investigating 6 market options.

During the 2025 legislative hearings, ERCOT presented demand forecasts that clearly
demonstrate the urgency of developing a market solution capable of supporting the
construction of new dispatchable generation. The Commission has adopted the ERCOT
Reliability Standard, and ERCOT’s modeling will determine the amount of new capacity
required to meet that standard. Given these conditions, I believe LSERO with Bilateral
Contracting offers a practical, competitive, and Texas‑appropriate path forward.

As outlined in my filing in Project No. 58777, LSERO with Bilateral Contracting creates a
uniquely competitive structure in which wholesale competition directly “feeds” into retail
competition. Unlike centralized capacity markets that produce a single clearing price,
LSERO with Bilateral Contracting allows each LSE to procure its own reliability obligation
from any qualified supplier. Because every LSE has a different load shape, a different mix
of renewables, storage, and demand‑side resources, and a different risk profile, each
bilateral contract reflects unique competitive conditions. GENCOs must compete for each
LSE’s business, and any seller that attempts to overprice will simply lose contracts to
rivals or new entrants.

While no market can ever be entirely free of market‑power influences, the LSERO with
Bilateral Contracting is highly resistant to them. The decentralized nature of bilateral
procurement, the diversity of LSE needs, the ability of LSEs to contract with multiple
suppliers or individual units, and the constant threat of new entry all work together to
 prevent any single seller from dominating the market. Combined with oversight from the
IMM, ERCOT, and federal antitrust authorities, this structure minimizes the potential for
market‑power abuse far more effectively than centralized capacity markets.

Given the urgency of ERCOT’s demand projections and the need for a market design that
can reliably support new generation investment, I respectfully request that the
Commission refer the LSERO with Bilateral‑Contracting to ERCOT for technical review,
modeling, and stakeholder input. ERCOT is best positioned to evaluate how this framework
would interact with the Reliability Standard, accreditation methods, and system planning
processes.

Thank you for your consideration and for your continued leadership in reliability and
market design. I am available to answer questions by phone or in writing at the
Commission’s request, but I am not seeking to testify in person unless needed to do so.

Respectfully submitted,

Thomas L. Darte

10503 Woodland Dr.

Greenville, Texas 75402
